We did that for state dinners or we did that for dignitaries that would come in, but ... at lunchtime when the president would be in the Oval Office by himself, [he'd say] 'Lemme have a tuna sandwich.' " At L'Ecosse, tuna and warm cookies are on the menu. Keeping with his Scottish upbringing, David's menu also is largely UK-centric: meat pies and fish and chips are two of the specialties. MINNEAPOLIS, Minnesota (CNN) — David and Christina Macfarlane had long hoped to own a restaurant. Given David’s experience as a chef at the White House, the couple already had strong culinary expertise in the family. Still, they had not expected to launch their dream during one of the most difficult economic periods in recent memory, and they were unsure whether it could actually happen.

Christina recalls the reaction from lenders: “The banks were like, ‘You’re opening a restaurant now?’” Her answer was, “‘Yeah, we’re opening a restaurant now.’”

David, who was born in Glasgow, Scotland, came to the United States with his family when he was in his early teens. Before long, he discovered his love of food. After finishing high school, he enlisted in the U.S. Navy, where he spent years working as a cook. Two of those years were in the kitchen at 1600 Pennsylvania Avenue, where he cooked for President Bill Clinton at the start of Clinton’s first term in 1992.

While looking at a photograph of himself with the former president, David remembers one especially meaningful moment. “He said that was the best meal he ever ate,” David says. “I was pretty geeked about that.”

Eventually, though, the Macfarlanes wanted more family time, which did not fit easily with David’s demanding, high-profile career. They relocated several times before putting down roots in the suburbs of Minneapolis, Minnesota. Most recently, David worked for Fusion Culinary until his job was cut.

Christina says that although David was upset about losing his position, she viewed the change differently. To her, it was “a blessing.”

“I thought, ‘Thank you, Lord! Thank you, Lord!’” she says, explaining that she believed the moment gave them the chance they needed to finally pursue their restaurant dream.

Now, even in a struggling economy, David and Christina stand behind the bar of their new restaurant, L’Ecosse — a name that means “Scotland” in French.

The economic climate, however, influenced the kind of menu they chose to create. Christina says they visited more than a dozen restaurants, studying menus and prices while keeping in mind the financial pressures facing diners.

They decided that although people were still going out to eat, they were not necessarily looking for upscale or elaborate dishes — the kind of food some might imagine being served at White House state dinners.

David says that assumption is misleading anyway.

“Comfort food,” he says. “That’s what the president wanted most.”

According to David, some of President Clinton’s favorites included nachos and salsa, tuna sandwiches, and warm milk with cookies.

“[President Clinton] wasn’t looking for any of the fancy frou-frou stuff,” David says. “We did that for state dinners or we did that for dignitaries that would come in, but ... at lunchtime when the president would be in the Oval Office by himself, [he’d say] ‘Lemme have a tuna sandwich.’”

At L’Ecosse, both tuna and warm cookies appear on the menu. Reflecting David’s Scottish roots, the restaurant’s offerings also lean heavily toward foods associated with the United Kingdom, with meat pies and fish and chips among the featured dishes.

David says he prepares the food using fresh, locally sourced ingredients. He is able to keep prices low, he explains, because he handles much of the work himself and operates with only a very small staff.

Every breakfast and lunch item costs less than $10. The couple says that once their liquor license is approved and they add a full dinner menu, they hope to keep dinner prices comparably affordable.

“The reason we did that was so nobody had sticker shock,” David says. “They’re very good items, but they’re also inexpensive items and you’re not going to break the bank.”

“If you want to come in and get Bill Clinton’s favorite, it doesn’t have to be $15 during the day,” he adds. “And that’s what we want people to understand — we understand where you’re at.”

Christina describes the restaurant’s approach simply: “You are going to get great food that your mother used to make for you.”

And ideally, customers can enjoy it without facing a painful bill.

counterfactuals.output:
**Former White House chef brings affordable Scottish comfort food to Minneapolis**

*Minneapolis, Minnesota* — On a cold evening in south Minneapolis, the smell of butter, onions and slow-cooked beef drifts from a small kitchen where a former White House chef is plating food that feels far removed from state dinners and formal receptions.

There are no chandeliers here, no rows of polished silver, no guest list filled with presidents and prime ministers.

Instead, there is shepherd’s pie, Scotch eggs, bowls of hearty soup and plates priced with the neighborhood in mind.

For chef **[Name]** and his wife, **[Name]**, opening an affordable Scottish restaurant in the middle of a recession might seem like an unlikely gamble. But the couple says the timing is exactly why they did it.

“People still need a place to sit down, feel welcome and eat something made with care,” the chef said. “Maybe especially now.”

After years cooking in one of the most high-profile kitchens in the country, he has traded the pressure of presidential meals for the steady rhythm of a neighborhood restaurant. His wife works the front of the house, greeting regulars by name, pouring tea, explaining the menu and making sure no one feels rushed.

The restaurant’s concept is simple: Scottish-inspired comfort food at prices working families can afford.

That mission has taken on new meaning as Minneapolis residents, like much of the country, face job losses, shrinking paychecks and uncertainty brought on by the recession. Dining out has become a luxury for many families, and restaurants across the city have struggled to keep their doors open.

But the couple believed there was room for a different kind of place — one that did not ask customers to choose between quality and affordability.

“We didn’t want to open a special-occasion restaurant,” his wife said. “We wanted people to come in on a Tuesday night because they needed something warm, filling and familiar.”

The menu reflects that philosophy. Traditional Scottish dishes sit alongside Midwestern-friendly staples, with portions designed to satisfy and prices kept low. The couple says they have worked carefully with suppliers, limited waste and built the menu around humble ingredients — potatoes, cabbage, oats, root vegetables and less expensive cuts of meat transformed through time and technique.

It is the kind of cooking the chef says he has always respected.

“At the White House, you learn precision,” he said. “But you also learn that food is about people. Whether you’re serving a head of state or a family trying to stretch a paycheck, the goal is the same: make them feel cared for.”

That sense of care is part of what drew customers in during the restaurant’s first weeks. Some came out of curiosity, intrigued by the idea of a White House chef cooking haggis and meat pies in Minneapolis. Others came because the prices were manageable. Many have returned because the place feels personal.

At one table, a couple shared a plate of fish and chips. Nearby, a father helped his child cut into a sausage roll. A group of older diners lingered over dessert, talking quietly as snow collected outside the window.

“It feels like someone’s home,” one customer said. “And right now, that matters.”

The restaurant is also a family project in the truest sense. The chef and his wife spent months planning the space, testing recipes and debating how to balance authenticity with accessibility. They painted walls, chose the music and built a menu that reflects both his professional experience and her sense of hospitality.

There have been challenges. Food costs fluctuate. Customers are cautious. Every empty table is a reminder of the difficult economy. But the couple says they remain optimistic.

They measure success not only in receipts, but in repeat visits, full plates and conversations with customers who say they are grateful to have a place that feels generous without being expensive.

For a chef who once cooked behind the gates of the White House, the new restaurant has brought a different kind of satisfaction.

“In Washington, the meals were historic because of who was in the room,” he said. “Here, they’re meaningful because of why people come in. They’re looking for comfort. They’re looking for connection.”

During a recession, that may be the restaurant’s most important offering.

And in a city known for enduring hard winters, a warm plate of food — served without ceremony, but with pride — can feel like more than dinner. It can feel like hope.

**At L’Ecosse, a Taste of Scotland Meets Minneapolis Comfort — for Under $10**

*By Staff Writer*  
*MINNEAPOLIS —*

On a cold Minneapolis afternoon, when the wind comes knifing down the block and the sky turns the color of pewter, the front windows of L’Ecosse glow like an invitation.

Inside, David and Christina Macfarlane move through the narrow dining room with the practiced rhythm of people who have spent their lives around food — he at the stove, she greeting customers by name, sliding mugs of tea and plates of steaming comfort food onto tables.

L’Ecosse, their Scottish-inspired restaurant in Minneapolis, is built around a simple promise: hearty, familiar meals that feel like home and cost less than $10.

“We wanted people to be able to come in without thinking too hard about the bill,” Christina says. “Students, workers, families, retirees — everyone deserves a warm meal.”

The menu reflects that philosophy. Bowls of soup, meat pies, toasties, stews, porridge, mashed potatoes with gravy, and daily specials arrive in portions generous enough to soften a Minnesota winter. The food is unpretentious, but deliberate — the kind of cooking that depends on patience, seasoning, and a deep respect for simple ingredients.

For David Macfarlane, that approach was shaped by a career that took him from modest kitchens to one of the most high-profile culinary assignments imaginable: cooking for President Bill Clinton.

“It was a different world,” David says, smiling at the memory. “Everything had to be exact. Timing, presentation, temperature — there was no room for guessing.”

He recalls the experience not as a glamorous detour, but as a lesson in discipline. Cooking for a president taught him precision, he says. Running L’Ecosse taught him something else entirely.

“Here, it’s personal,” David says. “You see the person eating your food. You know when somebody’s had a rough day. You know when a bowl of soup matters.”

That sentiment is at the center of L’Ecosse. While David brings the culinary résumé, Christina brings the hospitality that regulars say defines the restaurant. She remembers preferences, asks after families, and makes the room feel less like a business than a neighborhood gathering place.

The Macfarlanes chose Minneapolis, they say, because it understood both cold weather and comfort food. A Scottish sensibility — thrift, warmth, practicality — translates easily in a city where a good meal can feel like refuge.

“Scottish food and Minnesota food have something in common,” Christina says. “They’re both about getting through the weather with something filling and warm.”

Keeping prices under $10 has not been easy. Like many restaurant owners, the Macfarlanes have faced rising costs for ingredients, labor, rent, and utilities. But they have resisted the trend toward higher-priced casual dining by keeping the menu focused and minimizing waste.

David builds dishes around ingredients that can serve multiple purposes: potatoes, onions, root vegetables, oats, bread, stock, ground meats, and slow-cooked cuts. Specials change depending on what can be sourced affordably without sacrificing quality.

“It forces creativity,” he says. “You don’t hide behind expensive ingredients. You make something good because you know how to cook.”

Customers have responded to that honesty. At lunchtime, the restaurant draws office workers, neighborhood residents, and curious first-timers. In the evening, families come in for inexpensive dinners, and regulars linger over tea.

For some, the appeal is nostalgia. For others, it is value. But for many, L’Ecosse offers something increasingly rare: a restaurant meal that feels both cared for and accessible.

On a recent day, David ladled soup into bowls while Christina rang up an order that came to $9.74. The customer laughed and said she didn’t know where else in Minneapolis she could still get a hot lunch for that price.

Christina nodded.

“That’s the idea,” she said.

For David Macfarlane, the path from cooking for President Clinton to serving comfort food under $10 in Minneapolis is not as unlikely as it might seem. In both places, he says, the goal was the same.

“You cook for who’s in front of you,” he says. “Whether it’s a president or someone coming in from the cold, you give them your best.”

**From the White House galley to Minnesota: A Glasgow-born Navy chef brings budget-friendly British comfort food to the Midwest**

*By [Your Name], CNN*  
*Minneapolis, Minnesota —*

On a cold Minnesota afternoon, the smell of gravy, fried fish and warm pastry drifts out of a small restaurant where the menu reads like a love letter to the United Kingdom: steak-and-ale pies, fish and chips, sausage rolls, mushy peas and sticky toffee pudding.

Behind the counter is a chef whose career has taken him far beyond the neighborhoods of Glasgow where he first learned the value of a filling meal.

A former Navy cook who once prepared food inside the White House, the Glasgow-born chef now runs a modest, budget-friendly UK-inspired restaurant in Minnesota with his wife — a place built less around fine dining and more around comfort, affordability and a sense of home.

“It’s the food I grew up with,” he said. “Nothing fancy. Just honest food that fills you up.”

After joining the Navy as a young man, he found himself cooking for service members, officers and, eventually, dignitaries in one of the most recognizable buildings in the world. The discipline of military kitchens — early mornings, exact timing and feeding large groups under pressure — shaped the way he cooks today.

“At the White House, everything had to be right,” he said. “You learned quickly that food is about trust. People are counting on you.”

Years later, he and his wife decided to trade formal kitchens for a neighborhood restaurant of their own. Minnesota, with its long winters and appetite for hearty meals, turned out to be a surprisingly natural fit.

Their restaurant keeps prices intentionally low. In an era when dining out can feel out of reach for many families, the couple says they want customers to be able to stop in for a hot meal without worrying about the bill.

“We know what it’s like to stretch a dollar,” his wife said. “We wanted a place where people could come in, get something homemade and not feel like it was a luxury.”

The result is part chippy, part café and part community gathering spot. Regulars come for the fish and chips, but many stay for the conversation. Some are British expats looking for flavors from home. Others are Minnesotans trying a Scotch egg or a meat pie for the first time.

The chef says the restaurant’s success has come from keeping things simple: good ingredients, generous portions and recipes rooted in memory.

“A pie and a cup of tea can fix a lot,” he said with a laugh.

For him, the journey from Glasgow to the Navy, from the White House to a small Minnesota dining room, has been unexpected. But he says the mission has remained the same.

“You feed people,” he said. “Whether it’s sailors, presidents or families on a Friday night, you do it properly. That’s the job.”

**After a Layoff, a Leap of Faith: Couple Opens Comfort-Food Café in a Recession**

When Clinton Harris lost his warehouse management job in the middle of the recession, he and his wife, Marlene, did what many families were doing at the time: they cut expenses, stretched every dollar and wondered what would come next.

Then they did something riskier.

They opened a restaurant.

“We knew people were scared to spend money,” Marlene said. “But we also knew people still needed a place where they could feel taken care of — even if they only had ten dollars to spend.”

Their small restaurant, **Harris Table**, sits in a modest storefront with secondhand chairs, chalkboard menus and the smell of onions, cornbread and slow-cooked meat drifting from the kitchen. What began as a response to job loss has become the couple’s attempt to turn a long-held dream into a living.

Clinton had always loved cooking for family gatherings. His favorite foods — fried chicken, smothered pork chops, collard greens, macaroni and cheese, sweet potato pie and big Sunday-style breakfasts — helped shape the restaurant’s identity. Marlene jokes that the menu is “basically Clinton’s plate, written neatly and priced for the public.”

“He cooks what he wants to eat after a hard day,” she said. “That’s the heart of it. Nothing fancy just to be fancy. Food that makes you sit back and breathe.”

But the couple knew that comfort alone would not keep the doors open during a downturn. Their menu strategy is built around affordability, flexibility and low waste. Instead of offering dozens of dishes, Harris Table keeps a short rotating menu: a few entrées, two daily specials, several sides and inexpensive lunch plates.

“We couldn’t afford to guess wrong,” Marlene said. “So we made the menu tight. If we roast chicken for lunch, we can turn what’s left into chicken soup or pot pie the next day. If we cook greens, they go with almost everything. Every ingredient has to work.”

Portions are generous, but prices are kept within reach. The couple offers half-plates for seniors, family meal bundles, and a “recession special” — usually a meat, two sides and cornbread — priced to compete with fast food while still feeling homemade.

Clinton handles the kitchen. Marlene manages the register, talks with customers and tracks costs in a spiral notebook she keeps near the counter.

“I never thought losing a job would push us into our dream,” she said. “At first it felt like the worst thing that could happen. Now I look around and think, maybe this was the door we were supposed to walk through.”

The risk remains real. Some days are slow. Food prices fluctuate. Customers count their money carefully before ordering. But the Harrises say the recession has also clarified their purpose.

“We’re not trying to be the most expensive place in town,” Marlene said. “We’re trying to be the place where a family can come in, eat well and not feel embarrassed about watching their budget.”

For Clinton, the restaurant is personal. The menu reflects the foods he grew up loving and the meals he used to cook when money was tight but the table still had to feel full. For Marlene, it is proof that a setback can become a beginning.

“Everybody talks about chasing your dream like it’s glamorous,” she said. “Sometimes it looks like washing dishes at midnight and praying enough people come back tomorrow. But it’s ours. And that means something.”

**Minneapolis restaurant L’Ecosse serves Scottish comfort food with a side of White House memories**

**MINNEAPOLIS (CNN)** — On a cold Minnesota day, the warmth at L’Ecosse comes from more than the kitchen.

Inside the Minneapolis restaurant, customers settle in for hearty plates inspired by Scotland — the kind of comfort food meant to fill a table and quiet the winter outside. The menu leans into familiar Scottish staples, including savory meat pies, bangers and mash, fish and chips, soups, and other dishes built around simple ingredients and big flavor.

But L’Ecosse is also serving something harder to find: stories.

The restaurant’s team shares memories from time spent around the White House, recalling the pace, pressure and pride of cooking in a place tied to American history. Those experiences now shape a very different kind of dining room — one focused less on ceremony and more on making guests feel at home.

**Watch the video above:** L’Ecosse brings Scottish comfort food to Minneapolis.  
**Related video:** How local restaurants are trying to keep meals affordable as food costs rise.

Keeping prices low is a major part of the restaurant’s mission. As diners continue to feel the effects of inflation, L’Ecosse has tried to keep its menu accessible without losing the hearty, handmade quality that defines its food.

That balancing act is not easy. Restaurant owners across the country have faced higher costs for ingredients, labor, rent and utilities. Many have had to raise prices, shrink menus or change hours. At L’Ecosse, the goal is to offer meals that still feel generous — food that is filling, familiar and affordable.

For customers, that means a taste of Scotland without leaving Minneapolis. For the people behind the counter, it means building a neighborhood place rooted in memory, hospitality and comfort.

In a city known for cold weather and strong local food culture, L’Ecosse is finding its place by serving dishes that are both distinctive and deeply homey.

And for many who walk in, the appeal is simple: good food, a warm room and a price they can live with.
